handsOnLab.brief: You will design a complete ringfence policy matrix for three application classes (browser, Office suite, PDF reader), then validate it with a harmless test harness that attempts disallowed actions on a test machine and records which are blocked. Policy design plus empirical validation — the operator loop.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every cell of the matrix has allow/deny with justification; the test log shows each denied action actually blocked; no 'allow all' rows remain.
handsOnLab.deliverable: ringfence-matrix.csv plus fence-test-log.md — the policy and the evidence it works.
steps: Create ringfence-matrix.csv with rows for Chrome/Edge, Word, Excel, Outlook, and your PDF reader; columns: ChildProcesses, RegistryWrite, FileWriteScope, NetworkScope, Justification.
Fill the ChildProcesses column: for each app, list the ONLY children it legitimately spawns (browser: renderers/updater; Office: none expected; PDF reader: updater only) — everything else deny.
Fill RegistryWrite: deny all except the vendor's own keys needed for settings; explicitly deny Run-key and service-registration writes.
Fill FileWriteScope: documents/downloads for user content; deny writes to startup folders, temp executables, and system directories.
Fill NetworkScope: browser gets web (80/443) only; Office gets none except the updater and collaboration endpoints you name; PDF reader gets none.
Write the Justification per row in one line each, referencing the app's legitimate function — if you cannot justify an allow, it becomes a deny.

On a test VM, build a harmless test harness: a PowerShell script that attempts (a) spawning notepad from Word via COM automation, (b) writing a text file to the startup folder, (c) setting a test Run key — all benign, all logged.

Run each test and record in fence-test-log.md whether your platform's controls (AppLocker/WDAC/SRP or your EDR's behavior rules) blocked it; where you lack the enterprise feature, record the expected verdict from your matrix.
Add a bypass-attempt section: rename your test script to match an allowed name and re-run — document whether identity or behavior stopped it.
Review the matrix for usability: pick one legitimate workflow per app (e.g., Word mail-merge, browser file download) and confirm your fences permit it.
Write the rollout note: pilot group, one-week observation, block-log review cadence, and the rollback criterion.
Read the finished matrix as an attacker: for each allow cell, write one sentence on how you would abuse it — then tighten the two weakest cells.
handsOnLab.title: Ringfence policy matrix + validation harness

Ringfencing is only for browsers; Office apps don't need it

Allowlisting answers 'may it run' but trusted apps get abused — Word spawning PowerShell, signed tools used as LOLBins — so ringfencing answers 'what may it do' by denying child-process creation, registry edits, unauthorized file writes, and network sessions for allowed apps
Ringfencing replaces the firewall
mockTask.explain: Name the gap (trusted-app abuse / living-off-the-land), the mechanism (behavior restrictions on allowed apps), and the concrete example (Word-to-PowerShell). Then offer the Follina-class example: a document abusing a handler to launch a process — fenced at the child-spawn or the handler launch. That shows depth beyond the buzzword.
mockTask.q: Panel question: 'If the application is allowlisted and trusted, why do we need ringfencing at all?'

notes.body: Ringfencing starts from an uncomfortable truth: allowlisting answers 'may this code run?' but says nothing about what the code may do once running. A trusted application is not a safe application — it is an application whose behavior you have not constrained yet. Ringfencing constrains it. For each allowed application, policy defines four behavior boundaries: which other applications or processes it may execute (child-process control), whether it may edit the registry and which keys, which files it may read and write and where, and which network sessions it may open. Anything outside the fence is denied and logged. The mental model is a playpen: the app is welcome inside, but the walls are real. Consider why this matters operationally. The most common endpoint attacks do not begin with an unknown binary — they begin with a trusted one. A Word document with a malicious macro, a browser exploit, a signed administrative tool turned against its owner: in every case the parent application is legitimate, allowed, and doing something it was never supposed to do. Allowlisting waves the parent through; ringfencing stops the abuse. Worked example: compare two policies for winword.exe. Policy A (allowlist only): Word may run. A macro instructs Word to launch powershell.exe with an encoded command — Word is allowed, PowerShell is a signed Windows binary, nothing stops the chain. Policy B (allowlist plus ringfence): Word may run, but its fence denies child-process creation, denies writes outside the user's document folders, denies registry edits, and denies network sessions. The same macro now fails four independent ways: the spawn is blocked, the payload write is blocked, the persistence registry key is blocked, and the callback is blocked. Each block is logged with full context — parent, attempted action, target — which becomes the alert feed you will triage in M07. Common gotcha: thinking of ringfencing as 'extra allowlisting.' It is a different question entirely. Allowlisting is identity (is this code approved?); ringfencing is behavior (is this action permitted for this app?). You need both because attackers defeat identity controls by borrowing trusted identities. Second gotcha: fencing everything identically. A browser legitimately needs network access; a PDF reader does not. The fence follows the application's legitimate function — least privilege applied per application, not per machine.  A subtle point: fences should inherit down the process tree. When a fenced application legitimately spawns an approved child — the browser's renderer, the updater — that child should run under a fence at least as strict as the parent's, not escape into an unfenced context. Otherwise the attacker only needs to compromise the allowed child to inherit its freedom. Define the expected child family per application explicitly, fence each member for its own function, and deny everything outside the family. The process tree is the unit of policy, not just the single process.
notes.title: What ringfencing is: behavior control for allowed apps

notes.body: The canonical ringfence-bypass pattern — the one you must be able to whiteboard — is Word calling PowerShell. Walk it slowly. The attacker crafts a document containing a malicious macro. The user opens it in Word, which is allowlisted: the gate asks 'may Word run?' and the answer is yes. The macro executes inside Word's process and instructs the operating system to launch powershell.exe with a command that downloads and runs a payload. Under allowlisting alone, every binary in this chain is legitimate: Word is approved, PowerShell is a signed Microsoft binary. The attack succeeds without a single 'unknown' file. This is living-off-the-land: the attacker brings no tools, only instructions for your tools. The family has many members — script interpreters (powershell.exe, wscript.exe, cscript.exe), system utilities (rundll32.exe, mshta.exe, regsvr32.exe), and admin tools — all signed, all commonly allowed, all capable of executing attacker logic when invoked with the right arguments. Ringfencing breaks the pattern at the behavior layer. Word's fence states: this application may not create child processes. The macro's spawn request arrives, the fence evaluates the behavior (not the identity of PowerShell), and denies it. Note the elegance: the decision does not depend on recognizing powershell.exe as dangerous — it depends on Word having no legitimate need to spawn children. Worked example with numbers you can defend: in a 200-seat office, Word legitimately spawns child processes approximately never — its function is document editing. So a deny-child-processes fence for Word has a near-zero false-positive rate and blocks the entire macro-to-shell attack class. Contrast with a developer workstation where the IDE legitimately spawns compilers: there the fence must allow the compiler family and deny everything else, which is more work but the same principle. Common gotcha: blocking powershell.exe by identity while leaving wscript.exe, mshta.exe, and rundll32.exe allowed. The attacker simply switches interpreters — you blocked a name, not the capability. The ringfence must cover the interpreter family as behaviors: 'this app may not spawn script interpreters,' not 'this app may not spawn powershell.exe.' Second gotcha: forgetting that the fence must also cover the payload write and the persistence. Defense in depth means the macro fails at the spawn, and if it somehow writes a file, the file-write fence stops the drop, and if that fails, the registry fence stops the Run key. Layer the behaviors; never rely on one.  The deeper variant of this pattern does not even need a new binary: the attacker abuses the legitimate binary's own arguments. The same powershell.exe that your admins use becomes the payload delivery vehicle when invoked with an encoded command — identity checks see the trusted binary, and only behavior analysis sees the attack. This is why mature ringfence design constrains not just which children may spawn but what arguments the sensitive ones may carry: script interpreters launched with encoded or hidden-window arguments by a document reader are never legitimate. When you write the fence, think in terms of behaviors — 'this app may not invoke script interpreters at all' — rather than binary names, because the names are the attacker's to choose.
notes.title: The Word-calling-PowerShell pattern

notes.body: Some attacks do not even need a macro: they abuse the document handler chain itself. Consider the general class, taught here without vendor-specific exploit details: a specially crafted document, when merely previewed or opened, triggers an external protocol handler or helper application that the operating system launches automatically — and that helper, in turn, executes attacker-controlled commands. The user did not enable macros. The user did not click 'enable content.' The document format's own features did the work: the application that opened the document reached outside itself to invoke another program, and that program ran with the user's privileges. This class is why ringfencing covers more than child processes. A complete fence for a document reader constrains four behaviors against this pattern. First, child-process creation: the reader may not launch external handlers or helpers beyond its explicitly approved set. Second, the network session: even if a helper launches, it may not call out. Third, file writes: the helper may not drop payloads to disk. Fourth, registry edits: the helper may not establish persistence. Any one of these breaking the chain is sufficient; all four together make the class impractical. Worked example: design the fence for a PDF reader against handler-abuse. Child processes: deny all except the vendor's signed updater. Network: deny all — a reader's legitimate function (rendering documents) needs no network. File writes: allow only to the user's document folders; deny temp, startup, and system paths. Registry: deny all writes. Now walk the attack: the crafted PDF triggers a helper launch — blocked at child creation. Suppose the helper is somehow already present and invoked — its network call is blocked, its payload write is blocked, its persistence write is blocked. The document still renders for the legitimate user; the abuse class is fenced out. The operator lesson is about trust boundaries between applications: every time app A can invoke app B, that is a privilege boundary, and default-allow across it is the vulnerability. Ringfencing makes each such boundary default-deny. Common gotcha: assuming 'no macros' means 'no code execution.' Document formats are programs with rendering engines; the handler chain is the attack surface. Fence the behaviors, not just the macro setting.  Note that the preview pane counts as opening. Many document-abuse attacks trigger from the preview handler without the user ever double-clicking the file — the mere act of selecting the message renders the content through the vulnerable handler chain. Your user training should say 'do not preview unexpected attachments' rather than 'do not open them,' and your fence design should assume the handler runs on preview. This is also why the email gateway's attachment handling matters as a complementary layer: the fewer crafted documents that reach the inbox, the fewer handler invocations your fences must survive.
notes.title: Case study in general terms: when documents launch processes

notes.body: Browsers are the hardest applications to fence because their legitimate function is the attack surface: they download untrusted content, execute scripts, and open network connections by design. The fence cannot be 'deny everything' — it must be 'allow exactly the dangerous things the function requires, and nothing else.' Start with child processes. A modern browser legitimately spawns renderer processes, GPU processes, and its own updater — these are expected children, ideally constrained to the vendor's signed binaries. What it must never spawn is a command shell, a script interpreter, or an arbitrary downloaded executable. So the child-process fence is an allowlist within the fence: the renderer/updater family is permitted, everything else is denied. Next, file writes. The browser legitimately writes downloads to the user's download folder and cache to its profile. It must not write executables to startup folders, system directories, or temp paths that double as launch points — so the file-write fence permits user-content paths and denies execution-path writes. The download folder deserves special attention: it is the highest-risk directory on the machine, and the fence should ensure downloads there cannot be executed directly (that is the allowlist's job at launch, but the fence adds the write-side constraint). Network: the browser needs web access — that is its job — but the fence can still constrain it: deny connections to non-standard ports, deny raw socket behavior, and log aggressively. The updater is the delicate part: the browser must update itself, so the updater binary gets its own narrowly scoped permission to replace the browser's files — and only the browser's files. Worked example: an exploit compromises the renderer and attempts to spawn cmd.exe. The child-process fence denies the spawn — cmd.exe is not in the expected family — and logs the attempt with the renderer as parent. The exploit's fallback tries to write a payload to the startup folder — the file-write fence denies it. The fallback's fallback tries to open a raw connection to a non-standard port — the network fence denies it. Three behaviors, three denials, one alert bundle for triage. Common gotcha: fencing the browser so tightly that updates break. A browser that cannot update becomes the vulnerability — the updater carve-out is not a weakness in the fence, it is load-bearing. Second gotcha: forgetting extensions and plugins as child-equivalents. The fence should account for what the browser is permitted to load, not just what it may spawn.
notes.title: Ringfence design: browsers

notes.body: Office applications are the most attacked and the most fenceable: their legitimate function (editing documents, crunching spreadsheets, managing mail) requires almost none of the dangerous behaviors. The baseline Office fence is strict: deny child-process creation entirely — Word, Excel, and PowerPoint have no legitimate need to launch other programs. Deny registry writes except the vendor's own settings keys — Office does not need to register system services or set Run keys. Constrain file writes to user document locations — deny writes to startup folders, system directories, and temp-execution paths. Deny network sessions except explicitly approved collaboration endpoints and the updater — Word does not need arbitrary outbound connections. Outlook is the exception that proves the rule: it legitimately needs network access to mail servers, so its network fence is scoped to the mail protocols and servers the business uses, not the open internet. Now the honest complication: macros and add-ins. Businesses run on Excel macros — the finance team's month-end workbook is a program, and fencing it naively breaks the business. The operator-grade answer is not 'allow macros' (default-allow for code) but signed-macro policy: only macros signed by approved publishers execute, and even signed macros run inside the fence — they still cannot spawn children or write outside document paths. Worked example: the accounting team's month-end macro workbook. The workbook's macros are signed with the company's code-signing certificate. Policy: allow signed macros from the corporate publisher, and the Excel fence still denies child-process creation and non-document file writes. The macro calculates, formats, and saves — all permitted. An attacker who steals the workbook and adds a shell-spawning macro faces two gates: the signature check (their modification breaks the corporate signature) and the fence (the spawn is denied regardless). Common gotcha: the 'enable all macros for the finance team' exception. That is default-allow for the most macro-attacked applications in the company, scoped to the users with the most sensitive data. If the business truly needs unsigned macros, the compensating controls are a signed-macro migration plan with a date, plus tighter fences (no child processes, no network) on the machines that run them. Second gotcha: Outlook attachments. The fence constrains what Outlook may do, but the attachment the user saves and double-clicks is a new execution — that is the allowlist's gate (M02), and the two layers must be designed together.  Do not forget the browser's loadable code: extensions, plugins, and helper objects execute inside the browser's context with its privileges. A malicious or compromised extension bypasses the child-process fence entirely because it never spawns anything — it simply acts. Your browser policy should therefore govern the extension inventory too: an approved extension list, ideally centrally managed, with the same approval workflow as applications. An unmanaged extension ecosystem on a fenced browser is a fenced front door with the windows open.
notes.title: Ringfence design: Office applications

notes.body: PDF readers look harmless and are historically one of the most exploited application classes: complex parsers, JavaScript engines, and handler chains, all processing untrusted input. The fence for a PDF reader is the strictest of the three classes because the legitimate function is the narrowest: render documents. Child processes: deny entirely except the vendor's signed updater. A reader never legitimately launches other programs. Registry: deny all writes — a reader has no settings that require registry modification beyond its own keys, and persistence via the reader is never legitimate. File writes: allow only to user document folders for 'save as' functionality; deny temp, startup, and system paths absolutely. Network: deny entirely — rendering a document requires no network, and the updater gets its own narrow exception. This is the purest expression of least privilege per application: four denies and the app still does its job perfectly. Worked example: a crafted PDF attempts the handler-abuse pattern. It tries to invoke an external helper — child-process deny. It tries to execute embedded JavaScript that downloads a second stage — network deny. It tries to write the second stage to disk — file-write deny. It tries to register for persistence — registry deny. The user reads the invoice; the attack reads the fence. Now the validation discipline, because a fence you have not tested is a hope. Every ringfence policy gets a test plan before enforcement: for each deny, attempt the denied action with a harmless proof-of-concept on a test machine and confirm the block and the log. Attempt to spawn a child from the fenced app — confirm blocked and logged. Attempt the registry write — confirm blocked and logged. Attempt the file write to a denied path — confirm blocked and logged. Attempt the network session — confirm blocked and logged. Then attempt the legitimate workflows — open, edit, save, print, update — and confirm they work. Only then does the policy leave the pilot group. Common gotcha: testing only the blocks and not the legitimate workflows. A fence that blocks attacks and breaks work gets removed on Monday morning. Second gotcha: treating the PDF reader as 'not important' because it is not Word. Attackers do not share your ranking — they attack the reader precisely because defenders under-fence it. Fence it like it matters, because it does.  Two legacy Office features deserve explicit mention in your fence design: DDE and OLE. Both are mechanisms by which a document pulls in external content or launches linked objects — legitimate in 1998, abused ever since. If the business does not use them, disable them outright via policy rather than fencing around them; a disabled feature needs no fence. If some legacy workflow genuinely depends on them, that workflow gets the full treatment from M02: documented, scoped to the machines that need it, ringfenced tightly, with a migration plan and a date. 'Legacy requires it' is a bridge, not a destination.
notes.title: Ringfence design: PDF readers, plus the validation discipline

summary: Allowlisting decides what may run; ringfencing decides what running applications may do. This module goes deep on the behavior layer: the Word-to-PowerShell attack pattern, handler-abuse case studies in general terms, and complete ringfence policy design for browsers, Office apps, and PDF readers — with a validation discipline before anything reaches production.
